analysis.one_liner: Requires Congress to approve every major federal rule before it can take effect.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or floor vote in the 116th Congress, sitting in three House committees until the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The REINS Act would flip how the federal government writes rules. Today, agencies like the EPA or the FDA can issue major rules ($100 million or more in economic impact) that take effect on their own; under this bill, such rules would have no force unless both chambers of Congress passed a law approving each one within 70 working days. If Congress did not vote in time, the rule would simply die. In a divided government where one party wants to block regulation, that default would mean most major rules — on air and water pollution, workplace safety, consumer finance, food and drug safety — never take effect, no matter how sound they are.
analysis.who_benefits: Large businesses that face costly new federal regulation — energy companies, manufacturers, chemical and tobacco firms, financial institutions. The bill also claims to serve citizens by making Congress vote on major rules rather than delegating them to agencies, but its practical effect is to give any bloc in Congress a kill switch over new protections.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Firms facing costly new federal regulations

how_it_helps.text: Defines a 'major rule' as one with $100 million or more in annual economic effect, a major increase in consumer or industry costs, or significant effects on competition or employment — and bars it from taking effect unless Congress enacts a joint resolution of approval within 70 session or legislative days, after which the rule is 'deemed not to be approved' [S2][S3].

Makes the approval resolutions non-amendable and gives them expedited floor procedures, but does not force Congress to act — inaction alone kills a rule, which benefits regulated companies that prefer the rule simply never take effect [S3].

Carves out a 90-day emergency window in which the President can let a major rule take effect (imminent threat to health or safety, criminal enforcement, national security, or trade-agreement rules), and exempts Federal Reserve monetary policy entirely [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary people who rely on federal protections: if a major clean-air, workplace-safety, food-safety, or financial-consumer rule cannot win an affirmative law in a divided Congress, the protections it contained never arrive. Costs of the rules the bill prevents would otherwise be borne by firms and passed to consumers; the bill removes those protections by default.
analysis.who_pays_short: Everyone relying on federal regulatory protections

drawbacks.text: The strongest objection: the bill turns congressional inaction into a veto. A divided Congress rarely passes any law affirmatively, so even rules that clear agencies and survive court challenges would die by default, paralyzing major regulation across environmental, health, and financial policy [S3].

An honest supporter would acknowledge that agencies and courts already review rules, and that some major rules are politically awkward but broadly supported; requiring a recorded vote on each one could hold Congress accountable, but the same procedure lets a hostile minority block a protection that a majority of the public wants.
The bill also makes all determinations under the new process largely immune to judicial review, beyond checking whether the procedural steps were completed [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated aim — making Congress vote on major rules rather than delegating them to unelected agencies — has real democratic appeal. But its design gives concentrated interests a cheaper outcome: rather than debating a rule on its merits, opponents need only ensure Congress does nothing, and the rule vanishes after 70 days. On balance, the costs to the public in lost protections outweigh the accountability gains, and the emergency carve-outs are narrow.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Judiciary, Rules, and Budget Committees and a Judiciary subcommittee, and no committee ever marked it up or sent it to the floor before the 116th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced July 25, 2019 by Rep. Sensenbrenner with five original cosponsors, and referred to the House Judiciary, Rules, and Budget Committees the same day [S3][S5].
Referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law on August 15, 2019; no further action is recorded [S5].
The Congress ended January 3, 2021 with no committee vote and no floor vote on the bill [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Businesses that would have faced major new federal rules kept the status quo, where rules take effect through normal agency and judicial review instead of needing an act of Congress; the public kept existing regulatory protections rather than seeing them subject to a default death clause.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Regulated firms; public protections stayed intact

for.name: F. James Sensenbrenner Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited five original cosponsors at introduction

for.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce
for.what_they_did: Long a leading supporter of the REINS Act concept, publicly endorsing congressional approval requirements for major rules

against.name: Jerrold Nadler
against.what_they_did: Committee received the referral in July 2019 and never brought the bill to a markup or vote; its subcommittee referral produced no further action

against.name: House Rules and Budget Committees
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no recorded action on the bill

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 16 cosponsors were Republicans, with no Democratic support recorded; with Democrats controlling the House and its committees, the bill never advanced.

industries.note: Major rules with $100 million or more in economic impact would need an affirmative act of Congress to take effect; in a divided Congress, most would die by default. The industry's gain is the public's loss in the form of environmental, safety, and consumer rules that never arrive [S3].
Agencies would lose their core power to issue binding major rules without congressional approval, though a narrow presidential emergency window of 90 days remains [S3].
